Preconditions: Application built with `next build`. Browser DevTools Network tab open with JS filter enabled.
Test_Steps:

3. Record the list of JS chunks loaded on initial page load.
4. Navigate to the Gradient Descent lesson (/lessons/12-gradient-descent).
5. Observe the Network tab for new JS chunk requests.
6. Verify a chunk containing 'three' or 'fiber' loads only after navigation to the lesson page.
7. Verify the loading placeholder text 'Loading 3D visualization...' appears briefly before the Canvas renders.
Test_Data: Route: /lessons/12-gradient-descent. Expected lazy chunk pattern: contains '@react-three/fiber' or 'three' bundle.
Expected_Result: LossSurface3D chunk is NOT present in the initial page load bundle. A separate JS chunk containing Three.js is fetched only when InteractiveDescent mounts. The placeholder 'Loading 3D visualization...' renders during load. No console warnings about large bundle size.

Notes: Previous failure reason 'eagerly loads / warnings' was incorrect. LossSurface3D.tsx itself imports Three.js at top level, but this file is behind next/dynamic in InteractiveDescent.tsx and InteractiveOptimizers.tsx, so it IS code-split. Verified in source: InteractiveDescent.tsx line 15 uses `dynamic(() => import(...), { ssr: false })`.

Title: Timeline scrub control updates trajectory and ball position
Requirement_Ref: FR-LAB-GD-003: User must be able to scrub backward/forward through optimization history
Preconditions: Gradient Descent lesson loaded. InteractiveDescent component rendered.
Test_Steps:
1. Open the Gradient Descent lesson (/lessons/12-gradient-descent).
2. Set surface to 'Convex Bowl', Learning Rate to 0.05, enable Momentum.
3. Click the Play button and let the optimizer run for ~50 steps (observe Step counter in readout panel).
4. Click Pause.
5. Note the current Step number, Loss value, X, and Y coordinates from the readout panel.
6. Locate the 'Timeline Scrub' slider in the control panel.
7. Drag the scrub slider leftward to approximately step 10.
8. Verify the Step readout updates to 10, and Loss/X/Y values change to match step 10.
9. Verify the 3D ball position moves backward on the surface to its step-10 location.
10. Verify the trajectory line shortens to show only steps 0-10.
11. Verify the TrainingChart updates to show loss only up to step 10.
12. Drag the scrub slider rightward to step 30.
13. Verify readout, ball, trajectory, and chart all update to step 30.
14. Click Play again after scrubbing back to step 10.
15. Verify animation resumes from step 10 and history after step 10 is truncated and re-computed.
Test_Data: Surface: bowl, LR: 0.05, Momentum: 0.9, Optimizer: Momentum. Scrub targets: step 10, step 30.
Expected_Result: The Timeline Scrub slider ranges from 0 to history.length-1. Dragging it updates currentStepIndex in the store. The readout panel, 3D ball, trajectory line, and TrainingChart all reactively update to reflect the scrubbed step. Resuming play after scrub truncates future history and recomputes from the scrubbed position.
Actual_Result: Scrub control is implemented. InteractiveDescent.tsx lines 139-151 render a Slider for 'Timeline Scrub' bound to scrub() store action. Store's scrub() (line 82) clamps index and pauses playback. Store's tick() (line 91) truncates history to currentStepIndex+1 before computing next step.
Notes: Previous failure reason 'No scrub control' was incorrect. The scrub slider exists at InteractiveDescent.tsx line 139-151 with label 'Timeline Scrub'. The store action scrub(index) at optimizer.ts line 82 clamps the index and sets isPlaying to false.

Title: High learning rate causes divergence with visual warning on non-convex surfaces
Requirement_Ref: FR-LAB-GD-005: System must detect and display divergence when loss exceeds threshold or coordinates escape bounds
Preconditions: Gradient Descent lesson loaded. InteractiveDescent component rendered.
Test_Steps:
1. Open the Gradient Descent lesson.
2. Set surface to 'Rosenbrock Valley' from the dropdown.
3. Note the LR slider max adjusts to 0.01 for Rosenbrock.
4. Set Learning Rate to 0.01 (maximum for Rosenbrock).
5. Disable Momentum toggle.
6. Click Play.
7. Observe the Loss readout -- it should increase rapidly.
8. Verify when loss > 1000, the readout shows 'Warning: Divergence! LR too high.' in red.
9. Verify when |x| > 20 or |y| > 20, the optimizer auto-stops (isPlaying becomes false).
10. Verify loss display shows 'NaN' when loss > 1e6.
11. Reset. Switch surface to 'Saddle Point'.
12. Set LR to 0.2 (max for non-Rosenbrock), enable Momentum at 0.9.
13. Click Play.
14. Observe that with momentum on the saddle surface, the y-coordinate diverges (saddle: loss = x^2 - y^2, gy = -2y causes runaway in y-direction).
15. Verify divergence detection triggers.
Test_Data: Test A: Surface=rosenbrock, LR=0.01, Momentum=off. Test B: Surface=saddle, LR=0.2, Momentum=0.9. Divergence threshold: loss > 1000 (visual warning), |x| or |y| > 20 (auto-stop).
Expected_Result: Divergence is detected via two mechanisms: (1) loss > 1000 triggers red 'Warning: Divergence!' banner in readout, (2) |x|>20 or |y|>20 or NaN triggers auto-pause in store.tick(). The Rosenbrock surface has a reduced LR max of 0.01. The saddle surface gradient gy=-2y causes exponential growth in y when starting at y=0.1 with high LR.
Actual_Result: Divergence detection confirmed in source. Store tick() line 139 checks NaN and coordinate bounds. InteractiveDescent.tsx line 60 checks loss>1000 for visual divergence banner. Line 161 displays 'NaN' when loss>1e6. Rosenbrock LR cap at 0.01 confirmed line 116. Saddle surface compute (surfaces.ts line 40) has loss=x^2-y^2 with gy=-2y.
Notes: Previous failure reason 'only convex bowl, no divergence' was incorrect. surfaces.ts implements 4 surfaces: bowl, saddle, rosenbrock, ravine. Divergence detection is implemented at both the store level (auto-pause) and UI level (warning banner). The saddle and rosenbrock surfaces readily produce divergence.

Title: Regularization Lab: capacity and L2 lambda control overfitting on noisy sine data
Requirement_Ref: FR-LAB-REG-001: User adjusts model capacity and L2 regularization to observe overfitting vs generalization
Preconditions: Regularization lesson (/lessons/15-regularization) loaded. InteractiveRegularization component rendered.
Test_Steps:
1. Open Regularization lesson.
2. Verify two sliders: 'Model Capacity (Neurons)' [1-30, step 1] and 'L2 Regularization (lambda)' [0-1, step 0.01].
3. Set Capacity=30, Lambda=0.
4. Observe the SVG plot: the cyan curve should aggressively zigzag through every yellow data point (overfitting).
5. Note the MSE value (should be very low, near 0) and Weights Size ||w||^2 (should be high).
6. Slowly increase Lambda from 0 to 0.5.
7. Observe the curve smoothing out progressively.
8. At Lambda=0.5, verify MSE increases but ||w||^2 decreases significantly.
9. Set Capacity=1, Lambda=0.
10. Observe the curve is nearly flat (underfitting) with high MSE.
11. Set Capacity=5, Lambda=0.1.
12. Verify a smooth, reasonable fit that balances MSE and weight norm.
13. Verify all 20 data points (yellow dots) render correctly on the plot.
Test_Data: Dataset: 20 noisy sine wave points generated with seed=42. Capacity slider: [1,30]. Lambda slider: [0,1]. Overfitting config: capacity=30, lambda=0. Underfitting config: capacity=1, lambda=0. Balanced config: capacity=5, lambda=0.1.
Expected_Result: High capacity + zero lambda produces overfitting (low MSE, high weight norm, jagged curve). Low capacity produces underfitting (high MSE, smooth but poor curve). Increasing lambda smooths the curve and reduces weight norm at the cost of increased MSE. The model uses RBF kernels trained for 1000 epochs with L2 weight decay.
Actual_Result: Fully implemented. InteractiveRegularization.tsx trains an RBF model with useMemo recomputation on capacity/lambda changes. Lines 32-95 implement the training loop with L2 weight decay. Lines 122-130 display MSE and weight norm metrics.
Notes: Previously marked 'Not implemented'. Component is fully implemented with real-time RBF model training, L2 regularization, and dual metrics display.

Expected_Result: The Q-table evolves through episodes. Initial exploration is random. As Q-values propagate backward from S4, the agent learns to go right more often. The 20% epsilon ensures continued exploration. The Bellman update Q = Q + alpha * (reward + gamma * max_future_Q - Q) correctly propagates values.
Notes: The epsilon-greedy logic at InteractiveQLearning.tsx lines 28-39 has a subtlety: when both Q-values are 0, it explores randomly (line 31). When exploiting, it picks the higher Q and then has 20% chance of flipping (line 38). This means early episodes are fully random, later episodes are mostly exploitative.
